paragraphs: Federated learning lets clients collaborate on training while keeping their data decentralized. That collaboration becomes difficult when clients have different amounts of data or computing power. A model that fits one client may be too large for another, while clients with little data face a greater risk of overfitting. This paper develops a Bayesian framework that gives each client a personalized model.

The approach uses Bayesian neural networks to represent uncertainty during local learning, supporting training on small datasets. Its collaboration mechanism works through priors over network outputs rather than requiring models with matching internal structures. This allows clients to exchange useful information even when their networks have different sizes, accommodating differences in both data complexity and computational resources.

The authors also introduce a differentially private version with formal privacy guarantees that do not require assumptions about the learning algorithm. Experiments on federated learning datasets report better performance than strong baselines across homogeneous clients, heterogeneous clients, and strict privacy settings. The contribution connects personalized local learning with collaboration across unequal devices.
neurips-2024-a-bayesian-approach-for-per.tldr: Personalized Bayesian models collaborate through output-space priors to accommodate clients with different data, computing resources, and privacy requirements.

paragraphs: Integer arithmetic offers a natural language for describing combinatorial problems, and adding probabilities makes it useful for systems that combine neural learning with symbolic reasoning. Two obstacles limit its practical use: probabilistic inference is computationally hard, and discrete integer values make it difficult to construct gradients for learning. The paper addresses these obstacles through a different computational representation.

The authors express linear arithmetic involving integer-valued random variables as tensor operations supported by modern deep learning libraries. The central observation concerns addition: distributions over integer sums can be computed using an adaptation of the fast Fourier transform that works with probabilities represented in the logarithmic domain. This gives a way to accelerate a basic operation underlying larger arithmetic computations.

Because the representation uses differentiable tensor operations, it also supports gradient-based learning. Experiments report improvements of several orders of magnitude in inference and learning times over the state of the art. These are practical computational gains for the proposed formulation; the paper motivates them against, rather than claiming to eliminate, the underlying hardness of probabilistic inference.
neurips-2024-a-fast-convoluted-story-sca.tldr: A differentiable tensor formulation uses fast Fourier transforms to accelerate probabilistic integer arithmetic and gradient-based learning.

paragraphs: A generated 3D object can look convincing while failing to stand upright. That gap matters when the object enters a physics simulation or becomes a physical print: appearance alone does not establish balance. Atlas3D addresses this problem by adding physical stability requirements to text-to-3D generation, with applications including interactive environments, robotics, and freestanding printed objects.

The method extends tools based on Score Distillation Sampling, or SDS. It combines a differentiable simulation-based loss with regularization inspired by physics. Together, these components bring gravity, contact, and friction into the process of shaping an object. The simulation loss makes physical behavior part of the optimization objective, connecting the generated geometry to how the object is expected to stand.

Atlas3D can serve as a refinement module or as post-processing for an existing generation framework. The authors evaluate it across generation tasks and validate resulting objects in simulated and real environments. Their stated result is self-supporting geometry, making physical balance an explicit generation goal alongside visual appearance and the user's design intent.
neurips-2024-atlas3d-physically-constrai.tldr: Atlas3D adds differentiable physical stability objectives to text-to-3D tools so generated objects can stand on their own.

paragraphs: Combining familiar skills in unfamiliar ways is a useful test of generalization. This paper asks whether smaller language models can improve that ability by training on examples that deliberately combine language skills. Its tasks involve writing short passages that exhibit specified combinations drawn from areas such as rhetoric, literature, reasoning, theory of mind, and common sense.

The authors use GPT to generate passages containing randomly selected skill combinations, then fine-tune models with 7 billion and 13 billion parameters. Training on combinations of two or three skills improves performance when the models must combine four or five skills. Those larger combinations were absent from fine-tuning, so the improvement goes beyond reproducing the same combination sizes used in training.

A second evaluation separates skill categories into fine-tuning and held-out groups. Models improve at combining held-out skills despite those skills being excluded from the fine-tuning examples. This does not establish that the skills were absent from earlier pretraining. Together, the findings suggest that training on skill-rich text, including synthetic examples, can improve compositional capabilities beyond the particular fine-tuning combinations.
neurips-2024-can-models-learn-skill-comp.tldr: Fine-tuning smaller language models on combined-skill passages improves their ability to compose larger combinations and skills held out from fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation transfers information from a large teacher model to a smaller student, but a large capacity gap can make that transfer difficult. Intermediate teacher assistants can help, yet training them adds substantial computational cost. CIFD replaces these assistants with smaller modules that regulate how much information passes from teacher to student.

Its Rate-Distortion Modules operate on embeddings from the teacher's penultimate layer. Each uses an information-constrained bottleneck, and adjusting that constraint lets the module take the role of differently sized assistants. Reusing teacher embeddings avoids relearning low-level feature extraction. A second component places an Information Bottleneck Module inside the student to regularize learning when many Rate-Distortion Modules provide guidance.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on large datasets including ImageNet. They also evaluate distillation of CLIP-like models using a dataset of 12 million image-text pairs. CIFD outperforms specialized CLIP distillation methods on five zero-shot classification datasets and two zero-shot retrieval datasets. The results support controlling the information transfer itself as a useful alternative to training larger intermediary networks.
neurips-2024-cifd-controlled-information.tldr: CIFD replaces costly teacher assistants with small information bottlenecks that improve knowledge transfer to student models.

paragraphs: A model can struggle when the mix of subpopulations changes between training and use. The problem is especially difficult when misleading correlations occur alongside unequal group representation: a model may learn patterns that work for common groups but transfer poorly elsewhere. CODA addresses this combination by changing both the learned representation and the training examples built from it.

The first component uses two encoding branches to separate correlations that vary from those that remain invariant. A decoy classifier and a decoder that reconstructs inputs help coordinate this separation. The second component strategically augments samples using the separated latent features. A reweighted consistency loss then reinforces training toward a model intended to generalize better under these shifts.

The authors evaluate CODA against state-of-the-art methods on ColoredMNIST and CelebA. They assess worst-group accuracy and the largest accuracy gap between groups, directly examining performance disparities that an overall average could obscure. The reported evaluations support the effectiveness of combining representation separation with targeted augmentation for the studied spurious-correlation and group-imbalance settings.
neurips-2024-coda-a-correlation-oriented.tldr: CODA combines separated correlation features with targeted augmentation to improve robustness to spurious correlations and group imbalance.

paragraphs: Average treatment effects can conceal differences across an outcome distribution. A treatment might affect lower and higher outcomes differently even among people with similar characteristics. Conditional quantile treatment effects capture such variation, but estimating them can depend strongly on how smoothly the separate quantiles change with those characteristics, rather than on the simplicity of the treatment effect itself.

The paper introduces the conditional quantile comparator, or CQC, to combine distributional information with more favorable estimation properties. Like quantile treatment effects, it retains information beyond the average. The authors argue that it admits more natural examples of smoothness and can benefit from simplicity in an auxiliary quantity, giving the estimator useful structure to exploit.

Finite-sample error bounds establish how the estimator can take advantage of that simplicity. Numerical simulations support the theory and show more accurate estimates than baselines. An application to employment incentives examines earnings across age groups and reveals variation in treatment effects across quantiles. The contribution is a different statistical target for studying treatment heterogeneity throughout a distribution.
neurips-2024-conditional-outcome-equival.tldr: The conditional quantile comparator captures distributional treatment differences while allowing estimation to exploit simpler underlying structure.

paragraphs: Convex reformulations offer a route to optimizing neural networks with stronger guarantees, but earlier approaches had been limited to small or downsampled datasets. CRONOS develops an algorithm for convex optimization of two-layer networks that scales to high-dimensional datasets such as ImageNet. Its contribution is to make this optimization approach practical at a substantially larger data scale.

The authors then build CRONOS-AM by combining CRONOS with alternating minimization. This extends the approach to multilayer networks with arbitrary architectures. The theoretical guarantee applies to CRONOS: under mild assumptions, it converges to the global minimum of the convex reformulation. That statement does not extend the same global-optimum guarantee to every multilayer network trained with CRONOS-AM.

Large-scale experiments use GPU acceleration in JAX and cover vision and language tasks, including ImageNet and IMDb. CRONOS-AM achieves validation accuracy comparable to or better than predominant tuned deep learning optimizers in these evaluations. The findings support convex optimization as a useful computational component for large-scale learning, alongside the separate convergence result for the two-layer formulation.
neurips-2024-cronos-enhancing-deep-learn.tldr: CRONOS scales convex two-layer network optimization, while CRONOS-AM uses it within alternating minimization to train multilayer networks.

paragraphs: Causal discovery methods usually begin with measured variables that experts have already defined. In many applications, deciding what those variables should represent is itself a major obstacle. COAT addresses that earlier stage by using language models to propose meaningful high-level factors from unstructured information and help design ways to measure them.

The framework pairs this language-based work with causal discovery algorithms. Once factors have been proposed, causal discovery estimates relationships among them and sends feedback to the language model. The model then refines its factors, creating an iterative exchange between defining the variables and analyzing their relationships. The authors provide a theoretical result showing that the constructed feedback also helps the factor-proposal process.

Evaluation uses curated synthetic and real-world benchmarks, including human reviews and diagnosis involving neuropathic conditions and brain tumors. The reported experiments show significant improvements and support COAT's effectiveness and reliability. The broader contribution is a workflow that connects extracting candidate concepts from messy data with the structured analysis needed to investigate causal relationships.
neurips-2024-discovery-of-the-hidden-wor.tldr: COAT combines language-model factor proposals with causal-discovery feedback to iteratively improve the variables used for causal analysis.

paragraphs: Expanding a dataset can improve learning without collecting and labeling every additional example by hand. Simple image transformations provide limited variation, while synthetic images can introduce substantially new content. The difficulty is keeping that new content aligned with the original data distribution: generated examples that drift away from it can hurt the model being trained.

DistDiff is a training-free expansion framework that guides diffusion generation using information about the real dataset. It constructs hierarchical prototypes to approximate the dataset's distribution. These prototypes supply hierarchical energy guidance that optimizes latent data points within the diffusion model, steering generation toward samples consistent with the data being expanded.

The authors report accuracy improvements across diverse datasets compared with training on the original data alone. DistDiff also consistently outperforms the evaluated synthesis-based expansion methods and works alongside common transformation-based augmentation. Expanded datasets show robustness across different model architectures. These results support guiding synthetic diversity with distribution information, so expansion supplies new examples while retaining a useful connection to the original learning problem.
neurips-2024-distribution-aware-data-exp.tldr: DistDiff guides diffusion models with hierarchical dataset prototypes to generate useful, distribution-consistent training examples.

paragraphs: Adversarial visual patterns can cause pedestrian detectors to miss people, making them useful for studying detector robustness. Existing patterns often become less effective at medium and long viewing distances in physical settings. This paper investigates why performance changes with distance and introduces Full Distance Attack, or FDA, to address the identified problems.

The authors distinguish two challenges. First, a simulated view of a distant pattern can differ from how the physical pattern actually appears, so optimization may improve the wrong visual representation. Second, the adversarial objectives associated with different distances can conflict. A change that helps at one distance can therefore complicate optimization across the full set of distances.

FDA is designed to address both challenges. Physical-world experiments demonstrate effective patterns across several detector architectures, including YOLOv5, Deformable-DETR, and Mask RCNN. The findings show why robustness evaluation needs to consider viewing distance and the match between simulation and physical appearance. The reported evidence establishes effectiveness in the tested settings, rather than a guarantee of evasion at every possible distance or against every detector.
neurips-2024-full-distance-evasion-of-pe.tldr: FDA addresses simulation mismatch and conflicting distance-specific objectives to improve physical adversarial patterns across viewing distances.

paragraphs: Universal adversarial perturbations are shared input modifications intended to mislead a model across many examples. They are typically developed where the classification task remains the same during training and testing. This paper studies why that setup transfers poorly to few-shot learning, where downstream classification tasks can differ from those used to develop the perturbation.

The authors identify two obstacles: task shift and semantic shift. Their Few-Shot Attacking Framework, or FSAFW, addresses task shift by bringing proxy tasks into alignment with downstream tasks. It addresses semantic shift by drawing on the generalization abilities of pretrained encoders. Together, these components aim to make a shared perturbation transfer across changing tasks and semantic content.

The framework generates perturbations across multiple few-shot learning training paradigms and downstream tasks. The authors report state-of-the-art attack performance and an improvement of over 16% relative to the baseline method, without specifying the percentage convention in the abstract. The result highlights a robustness issue particular to changing-task settings: evaluating a universal perturbation on one fixed classification problem may not reveal its behavior in few-shot learning.
neurips-2024-generate-universal-adversar.tldr: FSAFW improves universal adversarial perturbation transfer in few-shot learning by addressing both task and semantic shifts.

paragraphs: Training a detector for fabricated or misleading language-model outputs usually requires examples labeled as truthful or hallucinated. Obtaining enough such labels is a major obstacle. HaloScope instead uses the unlabeled outputs that already accumulate when a language model is deployed, treating this naturally occurring mixture of accurate and inaccurate generations as a learning resource.

The framework introduces an automated scoring function to distinguish truthful from untruthful outputs within that mixture. Those scores then enable training a binary classifier for hallucination detection. The core contribution is the connection between mixed, unlabeled deployment data and a trainable detection model, reducing dependence on a separately collected and manually annotated dataset.

The authors report that HaloScope outperforms competitive alternatives by a significant margin in extensive experiments. Its practical appeal comes from using generations already available through deployment without requiring extra data collection or human annotation. These findings support the usefulness of unlabeled model outputs for learning a detector; the automated scoring stage supplies the distinction that would otherwise need to come from labeled examples.
neurips-2024-haloscope-harnessing-unlabe.tldr: HaloScope learns a hallucination detector from automatically scored, unlabeled language-model outputs without additional human annotation.

paragraphs: Causal disentanglement seeks to recover hidden causal factors from observed data. Existing identification results often assume access to interventions on individual hidden factors, an assumption that can be difficult to justify when those factors are not directly accessible. This paper asks what can be recovered from observations alone and gives both a positive result and a boundary on that recovery.

The analysis considers nonlinear causal models with additive Gaussian noise and linear mixing into the observations. Within this setting, it requires neither interventions nor restrictions on the causal graph. The authors show that causal variables can be identified up to transformations within layers, and that further disentanglement is impossible. The result therefore specifies the remaining ambiguity rather than claiming unique recovery of every hidden variable.

The authors turn the characterization into an algorithm that solves a quadratic program using an estimate of the observed-data score. Simulations support the theoretical guarantees and demonstrate meaningful causal representations learned from observations alone. The contribution links an explicit model class, its exact identification limits, and a practical procedure for recovering the structure that is identifiable.
neurips-2024-identifiability-guarantees-.tldr: Under additive Gaussian noise and linear mixing, observational data identify latent causal variables up to layer-wise transformations, but no further.

paragraphs: Learning coordination from scratch becomes difficult as a multiagent system grows, because the number of interactions and the size of the learning problem expand rapidly. This paper asks whether imperfect human knowledge can help agents learn more efficiently. Its hhk-MARL framework combines abstract human guidance with hierarchical reinforcement learning to support coordination among many agents.

The framework represents suboptimal human knowledge through fuzzy logic, allowing guidance to express less rigid rules. Agents retain the ability to decide how to use that prior knowledge. A graph-based group controller provides an additional mechanism for coordinating agents. The overall system is trained end to end and is designed to work with multiple existing reinforcement learning algorithms.

Experiments use challenging StarCraft Multi-agent Challenge settings with IQL, QMIX, and Qatten. The authors report substantially faster training and improved final performance, even when the human prior knowledge performs poorly on its own. This suggests that human guidance can be useful as a resource agents learn to incorporate, without requiring that the supplied knowledge already constitute a strong solution.
neurips-2024-integrating-suboptimal-huma.tldr: hhk-MARL combines imperfect human guidance, hierarchical learning, and graph-based coordination to improve multiagent training.

paragraphs: Domain generalization aims to train on several source domains and still perform well on an unseen target domain. Improving on a straightforward baseline across many settings remains difficult. LFME approaches this by training a target model to absorb expertise from all the available source domains, using specialist models to guide its learning.

Alongside the target model, LFME trains experts that specialize in different domains. Their output probabilities regularize the target model's logits, the scores it produces before converting them into probabilities. The target model remains the model used at inference. This arrangement allows domain-specific expertise to influence training through a relatively simple additional objective.

The authors' analysis finds that this regularization helps the target model use more information and implicitly emphasizes difficult samples identified through the experts. Experiments across benchmarks for different domain-generalization tasks show consistent benefits over the baseline and performance comparable to existing methods. The findings support learning broadly useful behavior through coordinated specialist guidance, with the benefit demonstrated across the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2024-lfme-a-simple-framework-for.tldr: LFME uses domain-specialist predictions to regularize one target model, improving domain-generalization baselines across evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: Holding out test data is a standard way to assess whether a model will perform as intended. This paper argues that, for widely considered inference settings in complex social systems, current data collection practices can invalidate that assessment. The issue concerns whether the collected data justify conclusions about the intended task, even when a model performs well on a benchmark.

The paper presents formal impossibility results showing that the train-test paradigm is invalid with high probability for any risk estimator in the studied settings. This includes counterfactual and causal estimators. The scope includes variants of recommender systems and reasoning with large language models. These are results about specified inference settings and collection practices, rather than a rejection of train-test evaluation in every application.

MovieLens illustrates the argument. The paper also explains why naive scaling and limited benchmarks do not resolve the identified problem. It discusses participatory data curation and open science as possible remedies. The central implication is that reliable validation can require reconsidering how data are collected, because changing the estimator alone cannot overcome the established impossibility.
neurips-2024-no-free-delivery-service-ep.tldr: Formal results show that current passive data collection can make train-test validation invalid in specified complex social-system inference settings.

paragraphs: One-shot federated learning combines knowledge from distributed clients using a single communication round. This saves communication but often reduces model performance. Existing approaches commonly transfer knowledge through local models and generated data. When clients have different data distributions, their models can provide inconsistent guidance, while the successive transfers can discard information.

FedSD2C changes what clients communicate. A distiller synthesizes informative examples directly from each client's local data, and these synthetic distillates are shared instead of the local models. This targets two problems together: information loss from passing through a trained model before reconstructing data, and misleading guidance caused by heterogeneous local teachers.

Experiments on more complex and real datasets show that FedSD2C consistently outperforms the compared one-shot federated learning methods. The strongest reported result reaches up to 2.6 times the performance of the best baseline; this is a maximum reported gain, not a uniform improvement across all evaluations. The findings support direct synthetic data communication as an effective way to preserve useful local information within a single-round collaboration.
neurips-2024-one-shot-federated-learning.tldr: FedSD2C communicates synthetic examples distilled directly from local data to improve single-round federated learning under data heterogeneity.

paragraphs: Methods that transfer 2D segmentation into 3D often begin with small geometric regions called superpoints, then use masks from multiple views to merge them into objects. SA3DIP addresses two weaknesses in this process. Geometry alone can merge distinct objects with similar shapes, while the Segment Anything Model's tendency to identify object parts can split one object into too many pieces.

The method introduces complementary 3D primitives based on both geometry and texture. This aims to reduce errors at the beginning of the pipeline before later merging steps accumulate them. It also uses a 3D detector to supply constraints for an additional merging stage, bringing more information from the 3D scene into decisions previously driven heavily by 2D masks.

The authors additionally identify annotation quality problems in ScanNetV2 and introduce ScanNetV2-INS with completed labels and additional instances for class-agnostic segmentation. Evaluations across multiple 2D-3D datasets support the method's effectiveness and robustness. The work combines improved use of 3D information with a revised evaluation resource intended to make instance-level assessment fairer.
neurips-2024-sa3dip-segment-any-3d-insta.tldr: SA3DIP combines geometric, textural, and detector-based 3D information to reduce instance segmentation errors and introduces revised ScanNetV2 annotations.

paragraphs: Estimating a person's pose together with an interacting object is useful for understanding sports actions. Existing methods often enlarge the image crop to include the object, such as a hockey stick. That also brings in background clutter. TokenCLIPose instead works with a crop focused on the person and treats the interacting object as unseen.

The model combines image information with language-derived context for individual keypoints. Language representations help supply semantic information when a keypoint is occluded or lies outside the crop. This changes the information available for prediction: the method can use relationships expressed through language without requiring every relevant point to be directly visible inside a larger bounding box.

The authors evaluate TokenCLIPose on Ice-Hockey, test zero-shot transfer to a smaller Lacrosse dataset, and assess occlusion handling on CrowdPose. Reported gains over state-of-the-art approaches are 4.36%, 2.35%, and 3.8%, respectively. These results support the method across sports-specific out-of-crop prediction and a benchmark where the keypoints remain within the bounding box but may be occluded.
neurips-2024-seeing-beyond-the-crop-usin.tldr: TokenCLIPose uses language-derived keypoint context to predict human and interacting-object poses from person-focused image crops.

paragraphs: Generative models increasingly contribute synthetic examples to the data used to train future models. Analyses of this repeated retraining have found that collapse or stability can depend on the synthetic-data fraction. This paper adds another feature of real usage: people often select which generated outputs to keep, so the synthetic data entering later training are curated.

The authors study this selection process theoretically as an implicit form of preference optimization. If curation follows a reward model, they prove that the iterative retraining procedure maximizes expected reward. The generative model itself does not need access to that reward function, negative examples for pairwise comparison, or the data density; the analysis works through samples.

The paper also provides stability results for retraining loops that include a positive fraction of real data at every step. Illustrative experiments on synthetic datasets and CIFAR10 show amplification of the reward model's biases. The findings make curation central to the analysis: selection can steer future generations toward rewarded outputs, while also strengthening the preferences and biases embodied in that selection rule.
neurips-2024-self-consuming-generative-m.tldr: Reward-based curation can make iterative generative-model retraining implicitly optimize preferences while amplifying the reward model's biases.

paragraphs: A learning rate chosen for a small network can sometimes remain useful for a much larger one when the models follow particular scaling rules. This is surprising because changing network size could change the optimization problem substantially. The paper investigates this transfer through the curvature of the loss landscape, focusing on the Hessian and its largest eigenvalue, called sharpness.

Under the rich feature-learning scaling known as μP and its depth extension, the authors find that certain spectral properties remain largely independent of network width and depth throughout training. They call this behavior super consistency. Under Neural Tangent Kernel scaling and other regimes, sharpness instead follows substantially different dynamics at different model sizes.

By connecting the Hessian spectrum with the Neural Tangent Kernel spectrum, the authors argue that feature learning explains the contrast: it persists under μP but progressively disappears under NTK scaling. Experiments cover ResNets, Vision Transformers, and language Transformers, including training on WikiText. The findings offer an optimization-based explanation for learning-rate transfer through consistency in selected landscape properties.
neurips-2024-super-consistency-of-neural.tldr: Under μP scaling, largely size-independent loss-curvature dynamics help explain why learning rates can transfer between small and large networks.

paragraphs: Multiclass learning commonly replaces classification error with a convex surrogate loss that is easier to optimize. Full consistency means that optimizing this surrogate supports the correct classification objective. In the setting studied here, achieving that guarantee ordinarily requires a prediction representation with dimension roughly comparable to the number of outcomes, which can be expensive when there are many classes.

The paper examines two ways to work with much smaller representations. First, it formalizes partial consistency and investigates whether a chosen embedding satisfies it under a specified low-noise assumption. This provides a way to reason about when a low-dimensional embedding is suitable, while making explicit that the resulting guarantee is weaker or more conditional than full consistency.

Second, the authors construct fully consistent losses with low-dimensional representations by combining multiple problem instances. Their approach uses parallelism to sidestep dimensionality lower bounds. The distinction matters: one route studies what a compact individual representation can guarantee, while the other reorganizes the overall computation across multiple instances to recover full consistency without requiring a single large representation.
neurips-2024-trading-off-consistency-and.tldr: The paper studies conditional guarantees for compact convex surrogates and a parallel construction that recovers full consistency across multiple instances.

paragraphs: Learning object positions without labeled examples is difficult partly because a learned internal representation need not correspond to the actual positions. This paper introduces an unsupervised architecture with a theoretical recovery guarantee. Its learned variables represent true object positions up to small, quantifiable shifts, giving a concrete interpretation to what the model learns.

The allowed shifts depend on specific features of the architecture and rendering process: encoder and decoder receptive fields, object sizes, and the widths of the Gaussians used for rendering. The authors analyze how each affects the error. This makes the guarantee informative about the system's design, connecting localization precision to identifiable quantities rather than offering an unspecified approximation claim.

Synthetic experiments validate the theoretical predictions at individual-pixel precision. In additional experiments on CLEVR-based data, the method's prediction errors remain within its theoretical bounds, unlike those of the compared SAM and CutLER methods. The contribution combines an interpretable position representation, explicit error bounds, and experiments that check whether the observed localization behavior follows those bounds.
neurips-2024-unsupervised-object-detecti.tldr: An unsupervised detection architecture recovers object positions up to bounded shifts tied to its receptive fields, object sizes, and rendering parameters.

paragraphs: Reconstructing viewed images from brain signals connects neuroscience with generative modeling. EEG is attractive for this task because it offers portability, low cost, and high temporal resolution compared with fMRI. This paper presents a zero-shot visual decoding and reconstruction framework that translates EEG measurements into information a pretrained image generator can use.

Its Adaptive Thinking Mapper encodes neural signals into a space aligned with CLIP embeddings. In the first generation stage, a prior diffusion model refines the EEG embedding into image priors, while a separately decoded blurry image preserves lower-level visual information. The second stage supplies the high-level embedding, blurry image, and a caption derived from the EEG latent representation to a pretrained diffusion model.

The authors also analyze how recording time windows and brain regions affect decoding and reconstruction, and demonstrate the framework on MEG signals. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance for EEG-based zero-shot classification, retrieval, and reconstruction. The approach combines semantic and lower-level cues from neural signals, supporting several visual decoding tasks within one framework and demonstrating applicability across more than one neural recording modality.
neurips-2024-visual-decoding-and-reconst.tldr: An EEG encoder and two-stage diffusion pipeline combine semantic and low-level neural cues for zero-shot visual decoding and reconstruction.
